title: Fur: An Imaginary Portrait of Diane Arbus
full_review:
"Fur: An Imaginary Portrait of Diane Arbus" (Picturehouse) is a cinematically inventive, though (as the title indicates) fictional take on the acclaimed photographer (played by a luminous Nicole Kidman), circa 1958.

The film shows this daughter of prominent furriers Gertrude and David Nemerov (Jane Alexander and Harris Yulin) on the verge of transformation from merely serving as a stylist to her fashion-photographer husband, Alan (Ty Burrell), to becoming a trendsetting pictorial chronicler of societal pariahs and those with physical abnormalities.

The catalyst for her metamorphosis is her upstairs neighbor, Lionel (Robert Downey Jr.), a mysterious figure covered with voluminous hair from head to toe (the fur metaphor again), who unleashes her artistic vision, and with whom she enters into a mostly platonic, but sensually charged, relationship.

Director Steven Shainberg uses elements of "Beauty and the Beast" (especially the Jean Cocteau version) and "Alice in Wonderland" for this absorbing allegory which, if viewed in that light, tempers some of the undeniably problematic elements which necessitate the restrictive classification. He builds a good deal of suspense, especially as we watch Arbus venture into Lionel's apartment directly above her own, territory that is "forbidden" yet irresistible.

Given the tale's real-life foundation, behavior that in a purely fictional story (e.g. adultery, marital separation, Arbus' fascination with the seamy underworld) would rate as "objectionable" are dramatically valid. Making it further palatable is the wide-eyed innocence with which Kidman plays her part, even as Alice-like, she voyeuristically observes some bizarre sights.

The Lionel character, though fictional, is said to be inspired by a real person, and he is sensitively portrayed by Downey -- though as Greta Garbo famously remarked about Jean Marais, Cocteau's beast, when he becomes human, you may wish Downey, too, would stay beastlike and not lose his hirsute appearance.

There's a problematic suicide element, but that mirrors Arbus' own untimely death from an overdose of barbiturates in 1971 at the age of 48. Also troubling is Arbus' eventual walking out on her husband and their two girls, though, in its essentials, this is true to the regrettable facts.

Some may take even greater issue with such embroidering of reality, but as the film is based on Arbus' biography (the only one thus far) by Patricia Bosworth, who also co-produced the film, one must assume a reasonable degree of emotional, if not factual, authenticity.

The film contains full-frontal nudity, a sexual encounter along with several highly suggestive if nongraphic encounters, adultery, suicide, some instances of profanity, rough language and crude expressions, a mortuary image of a dead woman, and alcohol and fleeting drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
